The year consists of three hundred and sixty-five days, and the count of years as they are now reckoned is eight hundred and some. Some Persian scholars trace this chronology back to the destruction of Kard, and those twenty years of Abd's era are from that date. This is the Second Chapter, on the chronologies that Iran does not follow.

That calendar is the Jahiliyya calendar — this is the chronology of the Arabs, because the counting of years among the Arabs during the Age of Ignorance was based on great events and important occurrences that took place among them. Among these was the report of Abraham, peace be upon him — when the Ka'ba was visited and the elephant army was destroyed — and its account is recorded in the Holy Book, in the Sura of the Elephant, and it is plainly evident. The Arabs called the years "the years of the Elephant" and made it their calendar, and in that year was the birth of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him. The count of their months is twelve, and the beginning of the month is determined by the sighting of the crescent. But for every three years they made a thirteenth month — and God calls them "those who forget" — meaning they neglected it, and the purpose of this was so that the Arabs could manage their seasonal trade. They were cautious about this and never abandoned it. And when those sacred months fell upon them, some Arabs would declare one of them lawful in their sermons. And they would name and call their months: 1. Mu'in 2. Nasir 3. Haw...

[Month names/numbers:] Ramadan 8, Hanin Azli 7, Asam 8, Adil 9, Manza 10, Wal 11, and Yeh 12.

This chronicle records that in the ninth year of the Hijra, the Sura of Bara'a was revealed and abrogated, and its enactment was established. The matter of the Khutba was completed — a year and a month — as is known to the people of the pulpit, who for seven weeks calculated it rightly. For twelve years it was recorded according to reckoning, and as the years passed, the genealogies returned to their reckoning, as the judges and the nobility of Fadl al-Din arranged. The chronicle brought down from the time of Zanbut Ghali up to Hawas Chankar: it is not known exactly. The number eight hundred sixty-two complete — some say a thousand seven hundred — seven hundred and twenty years had elapsed. This is the Khwarazmian chronicle. This chronicle is attributed to Khwarazmshah ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Iraq ibn Mansur, associated with the region of Khwarazm. Its columns and foundations are based upon the Syriac calendar of Alexander, and its arrangement serves to determine the seasons of sowing, reaping, and harvest, so that from its invention to the present, one hundred eighty years have elapsed. As for the Roman calendar, this calendar belongs to the Romans, and this chronicle is recorded as one of the most reliable, for it is contemporary with Jesus. This chronicle is based upon the enthronement [of Alexander] and upon the Romans' acceptance of it. Its beginning is named after the guardian and companion of the right hand. Three hundred years have passed since its establishment, and it is close [in time] to others. In the last month of Kanun [December] it corresponds, and in the second month it is called Fuwadlus [by some], numbering five. The months correspond to Shattat, and the names of the months and their number and their days are as follows:
7 Hordos / 7 Warados / 7 Sardatos / 7 Farnahlon / 7 Bolnos / 7 Bosfos / 10 Awatos / 10 Satarbos / 10 Watrum / 34 Baramros / and Nazarbos / and Andar / and Zakar — the year of the Syrians and Alexandrian Syriac [calendar].

And the Jews of the Children of Israel and the Hindus, because over several years they add one intercalary day, they align their years accordingly. Its properties include bodily lassitude, heaviness of limb, dullness of hearing, dimness of sight, darkening and muddying of the senses, decrease of appetite, and increase of births.

The nature of the Saba wind is temperate, inclining toward wetness. The time of its blowing is from the point when the sun rises until it is veiled. Its properties include bringing freshness and health, and pleasant clearness. The nature of the Dabur wind is temperate, inclining toward dryness. The time of its blowing is from sunset onward. Its properties are opposite to those of the South wind and moderate. These are among the southerly winds that serve as companions, brought forth from the four winds. When they meet together they generate movement, and from them arises the essence of other winds, and together they strike like the form of a minaret that the Arabs describe, and thus the wind is made to turn and circulate.

And the demons go down to the sea and come back up, ascending like vapor, and upon returning they do so in such a manner. Likewise they descend to the earth, and their dominant nature is such, and like a candle they move. If an island is described among these: the winds blow continuously, they come and go, and they ruin things, and it is as if the middle layers never reach an end. The elements repeat again and again in a cycle, as if the air, reduced to a minimum, catches fire from the water and the water through the agency of air; and because of the coldness of the earth it acts accordingly. By God Almighty, who has arranged the sustenance and nourishment and has assembled it, and it is witnessed and attested — Glory be to my Lord for this wondrous arrangement, and what wonders God has created, infinite and beyond count.

Preface: On the description of the inhabited quarter of the earth, and the explanation of the lengths and breadths of the climatic zones and the description of its extremities.

The scholars and geographers have stated that the inhabited quarter consists of three layers: the first layer is the air and the pure earth — meaning, it is merely soil and nothing has taken shelter upon it, and the second layer is the sea — that is, entirely water; and the third layer is that which emerges between the waters, where the land appears and valleys and mountains exist. Thus in some cities there are hollow mountains, and the winds penetrate the cavities, and from the vents come smoke and oily vapors, and the interiors are not solid, and the outward appearance of the earth is spherical, and whichever mountain is greater in height, its depth below is correspondingly greater, and its diameter and depth are proportional. The ships cannot go beyond those waters, and between them, as if by a system, the world is arranged and made orderly. The apparent surface of the earth is protected, and the rivers flow upon it.

The text deals with geographical measurements and distances on the earth's surface, discussing the equatorial line (khatt-i istawa) and its relationship to the celestial sphere.

The dividing line of the equator runs from east to west, aligned with the celestial equator. The longitude of a land is its length, and its latitude is measured from the pole. The two poles are situated on either side, and the earth's surface, like the celestial sphere, is divided into three hundred and sixty degrees.

According to Ptolemy, author of the Almagest, and some scholars, the first measure is a parasang; according to Tabali, author of the Zij al-Ma'musi, and some scholars it is sixty-two farsakhs and two; according to Abu Rayhan [al-Biruni] and most later scholars it is the same number of farsakhs plus eight.

A farsang equals three miles, and a mile is a unit of distance. A nada equals six farsakhs, and a nada-unit of measure corresponds to a certain number of cubits. A unit on the equatorial line equals twelve thousand cubits in length, and its breadth is two hundred and eighty-eight thousand units.

Each such measure placed together equals one thousand farsakhs, and one thousand eight hundred farsakhs in total. A row like a line of eight palm-lengths would be its unit. According to al-Biruni's reckoning, thirteen thousand times a thousand farsakhs is the measure. According to Ptolemy's reckoning, nine thousand farsakhs is the basis of calculation, and thirty-seven thousand miles would be the result if each farsakh is considered precisely.

When distance is calculated according to the convention of reckoning from the farthest point and the mile is not counted separately, then according to convention: eight thousand farsakhs equal four thousand miles; and according to Abu Rayhan, six thousand six hundred farsakhs equal four hundred and sixty miles; and the diameter, according to another opinion...

To the north of it lies the inhabited region, and the equatorial line passes through it — its latitude is established at sixty degrees and fifty-five minutes from the equator. Its people are divided according to the classification of Abu Rayhan, who in his book describes it thus: the seventh clime, which spans thirty-three degrees and fifty minutes in latitude toward the direction of the cold and uninhabited lands. And if one follows what the learned Abu Rayhan has stated in his book, the equatorial line is at three hundred and twelve degrees, thirty and nearly some minutes toward the north. The waters there are thick and abundant, and it falls within the seventh clime, extending from the east to the region of the Caucasus and the lands beyond, passing through the middle of the islands, Killar, and the surrounding regions. To the south lies Sarandib, as mentioned, and the sea of the constellation Aries and the sign of Capricorn. And the sea reaches as far as the western Maghrib and Mustī. At thirty-seven degrees and forty-eight minutes, Abu Rayhan recorded seven hundred and thirteen settlements, inhabited and populated, divided into seven parts. The first clime is attributed to Saturn; its distance from the next clime is the greatest, and its affairs require much effort. Its celestial sphere is the largest. From the east it extends from the region of the Caucasus toward the land of Albania, passing through Baluchistan and India, where great rivers flow — like the Ganges and the Kanfu — reaching the shores of India, and the islands of Sarandib and other islands. The great sea of India reaches the regions of Hadramawt and Aden and other lands of the west. The Arabian Peninsula is reached by the sea, passing through the clime into the lands of the continent and Abyssinia. The Nile flows to the region of Denar, and the sea of Qirnat encompasses the city of Ghana and the gold mines. And in the western sea it terminates; thus is the extent of this clime described.

The latitude is cold and dry, at thirty-seven degrees — this is the Fourth Climate, known by the name Khata among the Persians, called Aqnab by Abu Ma'shar, and called Nashwi in the tongue of the Greeks. It extends from the east and covers the lands of China, Barbwan, Herat, Tibet, and Khata, and Khotan, Sanmapan, Kashmir, Panjshan, and Transoxiana, and Khorasan, and Quhistan, and Munis, and Mazandaran, and Gilan, and Iraq-e Ajam, and Kurdistan, and Luristan, and Azerbaijan, and Armenia Major — that is, Diyar Bakr — and Rum, and Armenia Minor, and all of Byzantine Rum up to the province of Andalusia and its border, reaching the Western Sea where the two seas meet. The longitude of the arc's entry is one hundred and sixty-some degrees, and its latitude is in the sign [of the zodiac] at twenty-some degrees and seven parts. And the last latitude of this climate is thirty-eight degrees and four minutes.

The Fifth Climate: it is lower in rank, and its connection extends from the east and covers the lands of Khata, Qara-Qum, Butnit, Kashgar, Hajj, Sanjab, the land of Ghur, the districts of Saqun, and Transoxiana, Bukhara, Samarkand, Sharvistan, and Ferghana, and Juja-siya, passing through the region of Aran and Georgia and Armenia Major — that is, reaching Rum — and the Gulf of Constantinople cuts through the province of Wizant. It falls upon the Western Sea and its arc's longitude is one hundred [and some] degrees, eight hundred and eighty-eight [units], and ninety-eight parts. The latitude is forty-four degrees and sixty-some minutes, and the last latitude is at the degree of Hamal [Aries], some fifty-some degrees — this is the extent of this climate.

The Sixth Climate: the Persians call it Kharastand, Abu Ma'shar calls it by the name of Burj [Tower/Sign]. Its connection comes from the east and reaches the sea of Yajuj [Gog] and...

It passes through the province of Qamun, Kamal, Farkhār, Mar'a, 'Abr, Saqīn, Bulghar, and Baksa, and the Dasht-i Hilāl, and reaches Alān and Charkass, and Khutlukh Iskand; in this region lies the province bordering Constantinople. And the city of the Franks, and the silver mines, are found there, and turning toward the Arab lands it faces a high region. The latitude is eighty-eight degrees and forty-eight minutes; this province spans several farsakhs in width. Its breadth at the beginning is forty-seven degrees and eleven minutes — this is the Seventh Clime, which is called "Harim-i Āmīn." Its length, like the other climes, is the greatest, and just as the fruits of the trees of other climes are known, from the east it extends to the land of Gog and Magog, and passes through the province of Kamal, reaching the shores, the settlements of the Slavs and the Saqaliba, and the region of the Berber lands and the province of the Franks. Extending westward to the sea, the world's clime ends there. If measured from its settled inhabitants, its length runs to several degrees, being thirty-three farsakhs and three-eighths, and its breadth at the beginning is three degrees and fourteen minutes, which amounts to several farsakhs; and its breadth at the end is twenty-five degrees. Nineteen degrees remain in the rest of the clime; it is twenty-five degrees in total. The entire region has its rivers, streams, and hundreds of tributaries, and its forests of wild jujube and mulberry are well known among the rivers. In this place are mentioned plants, animals, and the creatures of Sinā, up to the boundaries of the Seven Climes, and the various kinds of beings found there. The animals, if they grow white-haired, are known there, and in this region, on the side facing east, the climes border one another.

Sheikh Abu Rayhan [al-Biruni] mentions in the book of Tafhim, relating a narrative that has previously been considered regarding the measurement of latitude across the world: that for each climate zone, the variation in latitude changes according to the arrangement of days, and that the breadths of the climates during those arranged days expand from east to middle. The scholars of Nudbastan have recorded in their tables — and Abdullah and others have stated — that the sages hold it to be correct that the southern seas settle and the land draws toward the north, entering the sea, just as was established. Each year the land is transferred between the sea and dry ground, without being recorded among the continental forms. Saquba [a figure] answered on behalf of the judges — including Ahmad ibn Umar — that the arguments were invalid, and this is recorded in the works of al-Biruni, and Saquba is capable of it: so that the hand keeps the dry land in balance, and the land remains dry. The authorities held — based on divine traces — that if there were such extremes, like instances of rain and flat regions and stones were absent, then if flat regions existed, the motion would pull clouds upward. And if the land received water evenly, the ecliptic and the zodiacal sphere would be enlarged, and the sun toward the south would change, like a ruby toward the south. The land would be pulled toward dryness, and if it were southern, the sun's altitude would undergo a decrease. And if this motion of the earth were so, the west would settle in its image — as if the north were recorded — the world would vary between south and north, and it would be observed how great the distance of the shores in the sea is, from years of recorded knowledge. And the altitude of the sun at the first point of Cancer in a given place has been accepted [as a basis for measurement].

The dignity of the realm of Rome, and under its protection for many years it was maintained, matched in rank with Jurjard. It was consistent and all of it was confirmed and verified from authentic and reliable sources. God, in truth — now the distance of the Seven Climes, even if not completed to the fullest, if mountains, caves, hills, and other terrain were to be included it would be a true reckoning. And in truth, not even a tenth of a tenth of a tenth of the cultivated lands would be covered. Let us note the boundaries of longitude: the First Clime is three thousand and eighty-two farsakhs in length, and its breadth is one hundred farsakhs, and the northern extent is two thousand seven hundred and seventy-seven farsakhs and a half in length, and the width is seven hundred and thirteen farsakhs and a fraction. The breadth of all Seven Climes is fixed, and that amounts to four thousand eight hundred and something; two thousand three hundred and seventy-nine farsakhs and two-ninths, as recorded, and each farsakh being forty thousand jarībs, and each jarīb being sixty cubits by sixty cubits. The total distance covering all these extents amounts to nine thousand and five hundred times a thousand thousand, plus four thousand four hundred and forty-four jarībs and a quarter jarīb. As for the four cardinal directions of the inhabited quarter of the earth, in relation to the four natures, the zodiacal signs, the planets, their hours and their days and nights — the Eastern direction is of a moist and warm air nature, pertaining to Spring, and to the zodiacal signs Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, and from the hours the first, second, third, thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth, and among the planets according to Ptolemy: the Moon and Venus, and according to Abu Rayhan (al-Biruni): Jupiter and Mercury — to these it is attributed. Those who belong to it among the humoral physicians say its digestion is predominantly strong. The Southern direction is hot and dry in nature, pertaining to the zodiacal signs Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, and from the hours the fourth, fifth, sixth, and sixteenth.

And among its companions and those who love it, the planets of the Sun and Mars are not related to the people of commerce. From the animal faculties, it is dominant in the attraction, and the Western direction: its soil is reddish and dry, its wind is the Dabur (western wind), and the zodiacal signs governing it are Gemini, Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius. The governing hours are the seventh, eighth, ninth, nineteenth, twentieth, and twenty-first. Among the planets, Saturn is the most dominant in relation to the people of trade.

The Northern direction is cold and moist; its wind is the north wind, and its humors are phlegmatic in nature. Its signs are Pisces, Aquarius, and Capricorn. Its governing hours are the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, twenty-second, twenty-third, and twenty-fourth. Among the planets, Jupiter and Mercury are dominant — and according to Abu Rayhan, Venus also — and the dominant quality is that of moisture.

The First Chapter: On the mention of the three births — minerals, plants, and animals. According to what earlier and later scholars have said, the subtle essences of the lower existences come to be gathered and preserved between water and earth. Through this retention and compaction, thickness appears, and through the power of the heavenly influences, things come to move. If motion and sensation are present, it becomes an animal; if not, it becomes a plant. If it has the power of density and flow, it becomes a mineral. If it is animate and gives milk, it is an animal related to minerals or to plants. Coral, mother-of-pearl, and the like have their own rank — the rank of intermediaries. Plants are related to minerals on one side and to animals on the other. Among the first of these is the green plant (khidr), which bears oud wood, pearls, and produce year after year, and from it come musk and ambergris, and its benefits are many.

At a time one becomes unaware of it, and at its end is the palm tree, until it bears fruit again, and something settles upon it bound by the wind, going into chambers. The third degree is that of animals, which is distinguished from plants by having sensation; its beginning is the worm, which Jahiz and others have mentioned living under smooth stones, with its outward and inward senses being slight, and its disposition is good; and its end is the horse, which has come to resemble the noble animals, and is like a companion and dwelling-place — they have said the lowest kind of human is one who has a tail and has the stature of Adam but has no speech or reason. The rank of the human is the highest of beings, and the boundary of its limit is beyond this — we will speak of it in the section ahead. The scholars of religious law disagree about it, saying: "Be also in meaning shown forth" — it is not growth in minerals and plants as was held, striking animals and humans equally, and thus it is not necessary to draw an analogy from it; by means of animals and humans it grows and becomes ordered, and this meaning is a clear proof and evident demonstration, so that the totality of plants and growth is all brought forth, and the bringing of action is established, so that he who wills it and he who sets it in motion — its form is not conceivable, and no cause or instrument is needed, and whatever it desires it brings into existence, and whatever it wills it does — as Raziyy al-Din al-Muhit (may God have mercy on him) has said: "Rabbani — there is no judge but God, there is no ruling but His ruling; Pharaoh is not to be found, whatever exists of the gardens will not be found, the gardens will not grow" — "They have not grown except as they say — Glory be to the Most High!" Now we begin the enumeration of the first degree, in God's will: The first degree — on minerals and plants. Fire is of the same kind, and trees, and merchants, and mouths, and living things — nothing existed that had no place, no disease, no cavity — and it was kept confined in the earth.

And by another element it becomes mixed and produces much on that ground, and it is retained and the greatest or strongest compound according to its basis. If the weak one is present, nothing of use will come from it. Corresponding examples require that the compound be useful, and if it is on the margin it will be among the metals. And if not, it will be spent and if it is poured, it will be scattered and dispersed.

Chapter One: On the pain of metals. There are seven essences: gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, iron, zinc, and red mercury (cinnabar), and seven compounded forms. If digested from the beginning to the end, it is neither sufficient nor beneficial, and is not counted among the metals, and that is not correct, because the foundation is mercury and the basis is in the reckoning of the mouths, and the metals number seven, formed from sulfur and mercury, and through it strength and permanence arise.

The power and resistance of the elements from within their innermost nature determines whether they will be solid and rocky or liquid. Sulfur and mercury, both being pure and equal, sulfur being red, and when mixed together — just as worms affect sulfur in mercury and mercury is affected by sulfur — the heat of the mine flows and gives benefit, and coldness and dryness are provided. Over a long period pure gold is produced, and if these qualities are present, but if the sulfur is white it increases and if this proportion is achieved, then through the shining process it is purified and becomes smooth and refined.

If the ground of the mine is pure and old, mercury is pure and sulfur is well-compressed and if these qualities are present along with its basis from that ancient earth, and if these qualities are achieved, then through this burning power, tin is produced. And if both this sulfur and mercury are of the nature of lead, the composition becomes iron, and if both are present but weak, the compound becomes lead. And it is said that from both, seven planetary compounds, the active composition is achieved.

The red face comes from copper, the cold compound, and the composition of white copper comes from copper, tin, and lead. The wonder is that at the base of all three substances there is a dry essence, and when these three are combined — that is, brass from copper and tin — the best brass was that of Damascus, which resembles copper in appearance and has a value of four dangs by assay. Its test cannot be done except by blue vitriol and tutiya; and from every alloy, lead, and silver there is no standard for brass. The composition of the seven kinds — from gold, silver, zinc, and so on — is known, and they are called by the alchemists "talismonic copper," and the copper in use is of equal weight, and the alloys are said to be equal in weight to the sum, so each differs in weight by exception, as does lead. The dissolution of silver, iron, one of copper-alloy and brass in the month of Safar: the element, the nature — or call it gold, the color, which the Turks call "the shining one" — is more resilient, and its essence: from alloys it is not at all, and it does not burn in fire, and it has not been removed from its place. It is the greatest blessing that God Almighty has bestowed and granted to His servants. Yet those who hoard gold and silver from the world's treasures and silver have been forbidden by the master. And God Most High said: "And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of God — give them tidings of a painful punishment." And the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "Woe to the servant of the dinar, woe to the servant of the dirham." This is the saying of the experienced one: The greatest yellow of Isfahan is the answer of the horizons; regret is its traveling companion, its reputation spread far and wide. David said: "The striving of the generous is praiseworthy; wondrous are the days of its glory; how fair is the one who bestows freely; would that the night remained, its radiance would diminish not."

The poets of the school have composed in this context a quatrain (ruba'i): From a dear one whose silver and pain endure — the heart's longing remains — the fire of grief burns on — from a stone quarry they bring it forth, its charm and nature endure.

The world's axis, guide and corrector it is, and the phoenix shows the way — likewise:

Ruba'i:
O you who combine all pleasures, beloved of all, gracious and loyal — near you is goodness, a remedy for faults, fulfilling needs, of refined and generous nature.

Its second property: it gladdens the heart and brightens the spirit, strengthens the constitution, removes excess moisture quickly, sweetens the breath of the mouth, and benefits the eyesight if taken pure from the mines.

Concerning silver (al-fidda): It is called "nafreh" among the Persians, and "gümüş" among the Turks, and among the people it is known as the essence of gold — it fulfills needs and is of general benefit. However, prolonged use brings heaviness; it burns the constitution and causes nodules to form. Its taste is balanced, tending toward coldness and dryness. Its properties: it produces moisture and congestion, dissolves blockages, disperses flatulence, removes hemorrhoids, and benefits the heart.

Silver (al-fidda) is beneficial for scabies, skin eruptions, and itching. Al-Ghar Sabuni is well known among the Persians who call it "sabraki." Its properties are beneficial for facial paralysis and distortion; it is applied as a plaster on the swellings of the throat and jaw, and prevents regrowth.

Copper (al-nuhas): There are two kinds — one is red, of good quality; the second is a reddish variety seen in Yazd; the third is a red type found in Sabzavar. Its temperament is hot and dry. Its second property: it expels diseases, removes excess flesh, is beneficial, and mixed with foods such as oranges and sweets, its consumption is a cause of gastrointestinal diseases — and of henbane (al-hanbul).

Cancer, spleen, liver, and stomach — its temperament is [that of] lead; the Persians call it zarr. It has several properties; the best of them is that its whiteness near pure standing water [is notable]. Its temperament is cold and moist; its first special property is that it is beneficial for the stomach and for milk and dairy. It repels the disease of cancer, and if carried on one's person, it prevents nocturnal emissions. From this [metal] one can make collars for children on trees to strengthen the brain, and it is reported that its use is for clarifying [things], polishing teeth, and making them white. It is used for al-halila [myrobalan]; it is of humble value and very beneficial; it is known among the people as "qummus." No craft involving myrobalan can be done the same way in fulfilling needs. The guardian of the world is sustained by it, and [through it] the kingdom is preserved and the kingdom's ruin [is prevented]. God Almighty has said concerning iron: "We sent down iron, in which there is great might and benefits for the people." Its temperament is warm and dry; it narrows in the middle of the vessels and channels, and its dross [slag] gives life. It removes the buzzing from the ears and brings out [impurities], and iron rust [verdigris] is used. It is beneficial for menstrual blood. [As for] al-usrub [lead], its temperament is cold and moist. Its first special property is that it cleanses silver from contamination, and it crushes diamonds. Gold leaf and silk of high quality cannot be made without it. It is beneficial for scrofula and ulcers; like cow's oil [butter/fat], it is useful for [skin conditions], and it repels swellings and inflammations. The seventh [substance], when cold and dry, placed in lime — note that it causes slipperiness and [certain conditions], and it removes hair from women's bodies, and that [substance] is among the special properties of life-giving things. Section Two: On the mention of the refined atmospheric [phenomena]: the collective [things] that are produced from rainfall and...

Assistance [of matter] is obtained in the interior of the earth, and jasper is formed and retained, growing from it. In proportion to its first deposit in the depths, or however it is retained, the earthly elements have nothing against it. The heat of the mine and the length of time refines it, and clarity and purity appear; the heart of the crystal knows it has settled and grown, and according to the natures of the minerals their temperaments differ. Jasper varies, and according to the influences of the planets its color differs: black comes from Saturn, green from Venus, red from Mars, yellow from the Sun, blue from Mercury, and both colors from the Moon. The second type: water retained in the earth for a proportionate time, with the heat of the sun and the length of time, produces jasper, and it changes, becoming homogeneous, and the variation of its colors, natures, and properties corresponds to the variation of its mine. A mine that is moderate in itself is balanced; if the extraction from the earth is from the equatorial zone the gems are noble. The variation in it is due to variation in the mine, and its redness has a particular quality. If it settles in the earth like salt, it produces various salts and vapors and nothing forms. If there is a good substance in the earth it causes harm and produces various marks. If it is of high quality the vein becomes empty and dry, and in some places a fine water spring is produced. The gems there: fire burns them and does not allow them to break, and upon water they do not dissolve. Various vapors are present, and mostly striking them with fire is needed, but with gentle water the diamond, emerald, and ruby may be struck — with both water and fire striking is needed, and they dissolve further; others dissolve in water, such as salts, niter, and borax — their like is thus. Rubies and coral through animal intermediary become pearls; animals' natural processes produce what is desired. Amber in the air becomes more solid, and so it is.

The arts and crafts will not be spoiled — I will bring together things that have an affinity with one another, such as gold and diamond, which have a great affinity, just as sandalwood has with snake venom; and iron with magnet; and those things that are mutually opposing, such as cinnabar and lead; and those things that have cleansing power, such as sal ammoniac and grease — by these, fat can be purified. Mention is made of minerals according to their highest, middle, and lowest grades.

Know that the highest — the jewels that hold the highest rank in their properties and value — their first property: the pearl is formed in the heart of the oyster, which the Turks called "al-jawhar." It is obtained in the sea, in the finest clear and luminous waters and in the clearest streams. Just as the water is purer and sweeter, the pearl therein becomes more brilliant and lustrous.

It is obtained from the sea by divers who descend to the ocean floor, and those called "banat al-bahr" (daughters of the sea) retrieve them from the shells. These divers measure and calculate the shells, taking from them what they need.

The oyster opens like drops of rain falling into its shell, and when the pearl-gatherer comes to know the oyster, it is as if he has been entrusted with its care, nourishing the pearl within.

The shell rests on the surface of the water, and its mouth faces the sky so that the pearl within it may be properly formed. Thus the water enters into it, congeals, and through its interaction with others like it, becomes firm. When the throat of the oyster is sealed, the pearl therein, if the interior is clear, becomes a lustrous, smooth, and rolling pearl, bright and fine. But if something turbid enters it, the pearl becomes murky and rough in appearance. Pearls should be weighed and assessed in the manner described.

When it reaches the prescribed amount, the fifth is called, and when it reaches the weight, it is requested, and rupture turns it red — that is, it calls out, and a reddish sediment appears. It is mostly related to the sediment of the oyster shell, being unstable and floating; it rarely settles, and if it remains in the oyster shell, the pearl will not be split, and the other shell will be shaped by nature into a polished pearl.

In the first degree, its dry nature: its special property is to repel palpitations of the heart, fear, and vertigo. It purifies the blood of the heart, prevents the return of that blood, and strengthens the faculty of sight; it sharpens the eyesight, removes excessive tearing, stops hemorrhage, and benefits women. It brings stability, brightens the teeth, and the Arabs call it "Hajar al-Habba." It is beneficial for headache. Its range is long and elongated, and its color is tending toward yellow. If placed on the head with a paste of coriander, it acts as a sedative and causes numbness. When poured into milk, it neutralizes poison; when it falls into river water, it repels scorpions. If placed on a wound, it draws out the venom similarly. It cures snakebite and the bites of scorpions and other venomous creatures. It is obtained from five mines, and learned authorities have recorded this. It is rare and precious.

Second property: Among stones, that which is sometimes red — from these, the best three in rank I shall describe. The Diamond (al-Māss): in books of praise it is positively affirmed — the diamond comes in several types, one of which is white.

And it is transparent, remaining like that. Pharaoh's people would gather it, and others would bring it back. It is called by the people of Islam "red," and they say it is crimson-colored and black-colored as well, confirming this. The fourth kind, with its greenish hue, was noted; it is found in the mountains of Sarab, falling upon the earth, and eagles and mountain birds would carry it off. People would go and cast down loads of it, and the diamond would fall among them, and they would take it away. Several scholars and experts brought it out and carried great loads of it. Some said it passes through and does not stop, and Ibn Jabir also mentioned that in the hollow interior it forms the shape of a diamond, and some hard stones would break. Their fractions are like a third of it, and one cannot break it when lead is placed between the pieces. This stone, in hardness, is so great that even the finest steel drill cannot scratch it; the greed for diamond exhausts both. It is beneficial to those who work in mines, and when cleaned with mastic, it is good for the heart and does not harm the stone. When brought out in this way, with care, it is useful for strengthening the teeth, prevents tooth decay, is beneficial to evil-doers, and is a remedy. It is yellow in color as well, and when finely powdered with green and transparent material mixed together, it is ground fine: it kills poison and stops bleeding, improves vision, and is beneficial for the liver. It is said to prevent epilepsy, and if a woman who has difficulty in childbirth wears it, it is beneficial.

Agate (Aqiq):
By its bond, it quickly brings relief and is a companion superior to ruby. It comes in several varieties; the one with a clearer, more luminous red color is found most abundantly in Yemen. Its property is that it whitens the teeth; when mixed with tooth powder it cleans the teeth. It drives away the smell from the mind, removes cataracts from the eye, and is beneficial for palpitations of the heart. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him and his family, said: "If it were placed in the land of Zechariah it would make him happy." And it is narrated from the Prophet that he said to Usayas ibn Wasila: "Seal your rings with agate, for you are the nobility." And from Jesus, peace be upon our Prophet and upon him, it is narrated: whoever wears a ring set with an agate signet and has written upon it "There is no god but God, the True King, the Manifest King," and carries it with him, he should not fear. And we have established that such is the agate: it comes in four varieties and is trustworthy.

Son:
The best comes from Nishapur; it is not harmful, and the kind that bears oil and fat in it is injurious. In two respects it benefits the eyes and increases vision, and it is useful for all ailments; however, coughing makes it necessary to bear it. For this reason, people hold it in high esteem. It is reported from Imam Jafar al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, that it has been transmitted: "Sell it not cheaply — sell it high, sell it high." Weeping bitterly over it was once the fashion.

Ruby (La'l):
In earlier times it was well known, and for this reason its mention preceded others. Near Badakhshan, in the mountains, there are mines; earthquakes shook the mountains and cracked them open, revealing ruby mines. The color ranges from red to yellow, and much of it is green. The better and finer kind is the deep red Badakhshani variety. Its value is proportional to its clarity, like that of the emerald. Ruby is suitable as a companion to the yaqut (sapphire/corundum). It is warm in temperament and benefits the stomach greatly; it purifies and refines. It cleanses the kidneys; if its color is pale, tending to greenish and transparent, it becomes even more lustrous. It repels clouding of the eyes, and those who desire to wear it secretly should do so.

Then on Monday, following the pomegranate and the grape, red and pure, known for a thousand years, and in seven thousand years within the stone-vessel its property is found: the seeker is freed from plague, people do not know poverty or ugliness, and it brings water from the sky. Among its benefits, it gladdens the heart and is among the precious gems and jewels sought after.

The brother Radi al-Din Muhammad Tusi, may God have mercy on him, in a work called "Wonderful Things," quoting from Sheikh Abu Makaran, relates that the green Kachhanqal — also called the green grape — is a sky-colored stone:

Five parts: three parts of syringe-root, purified and combined, four parts Tusi-powder, four parts ground Sarjola, four parts of Karjubik powder, and one part white [crystal], with raqim mixed in equal portions.

The highest grade among them, at first rank, is free of conflict and quite green — slightly dark in color. Its property is that it treats chronic ailments, is beneficial to the eyes, is heard immediately upon use, and is paired with crystal in its rank.

It is of middle rank among the jewels, ranked at a moderate level; it is not found near us. We mention Sadaf (mother-of-pearl) and Marjan (coral): these two are amber-like, refined and fresh — coral is red and sadaf is yellow, red, white, and black — and they are found in the ocean; each has properties that retain and hold together, and strengthen the eyesight; they are beneficial in Egypt and Arabia; they reduce roughness.

It gives a smooth polish, clears the knot of the eye. Crystal — this is a pure kind. The best grade is the isfani type, and among them the finest is the Indian kind. Most of it comes from villages, and its property, when placed in sunlight, becomes warm.

Camel
The camel's teeth are beneficial for toothache; its spittle is not harmful to anyone. Agate — yellow, white, red, black, and multicolored — is beneficial, and some say it has drawbacks. It contains properties that attract bodily humors and desires. And the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in describing its qualities said: "The reward is ours and the gathering is for the common people." The sponge-stone is, according to some, a place of protection; it drives away urinary stones and is rare to find.

The name of the stone repels, and it keeps people from harm; if it is present in an assembly, it prevents conflict. If it is present, it removes blisters, relieves thirst, and brings benefit.

Suleiman ibn Abd al-Malik said: "The kingdom belongs to no one except through virtue." The kingdom of Solomon son of David — some say: "If your court's wealth is more, then your kingdom is greater." This was the case because Asaf ibn Barkhiya was his vizier, and he had a connection to Solomon. The vizier publicized Solomon's virtues, and he sent Ja'far al-Munajjim as an envoy. He was sent to listen and act as an ambassador to the kings, to transform the land of the Jews into the dominion of Islam and take charge of the great house. This was connected to those great ones, and through various virtues he gained influence and honor among them. He was summoned to Damascus and praised as an expert in astronomy; he served the sultan and was kept in iron chains. Solomon the Red remained his guardian, and was kept in the service of the great king. When he came, he told him in response: "If you do what I say, I will act accordingly." The name was then given, and through great effort Solomon established the community. It is attributed to Zuhair al-Jafari, whose lineage is connected to water — "from among the ungrateful." He clothed them and gathered them, and then finished with them, reproaching and driving them away. They expelled them, and the people of Burqan, whose small stones come from Abraham.

They find the afterbirth, and out of desire for that child's afterbirth, they anoint it with saffron and bring it along. As for Abbas — it is placed before him as a remedy for jaundice: bring it and apply it to the ears. The Indians carry it with them and observe it. It is called "Qadizahr" — the Arabs call it "Sunush." It comes in several varieties: one is green-tinged, one is slightly yellowish, one is whitish, and one is the darkest and most yellowish. Its weight and surface properties are such that if rubbed with oil and given to drink, it repels the biting of scorpions and other venomous creatures, and if it is placed on a bone wound, it heals it. It is said that "Karya" — according to one opinion — is the gum of the jujube tree, and it is like mastic. It is gathered from the licorice plant and from the grass called "Farq" — according to one opinion it is the mineral called "Kalbi stone," meaning: it is used as a remedy. Its properties include: it relieves palpitations of the heart, benefits the throat, removes fear and anxiety. It is safe from harm and beneficial to the stomach and intestines — so says al-Adwani. According to the jeweler, its property is to repel bitter fever; the people of Hawlan and Kapur say it is a remedy. According to the school of al-Harwani, two varieties of it are known. It benefits young men and is used in youth. They call it "Hajar al-Baqar" (stone of the ox) — it is found in abundance and they call it "Kawran." It is a gum from a tree and is similar to it. If placed in the midst of poison, it counteracts the thirst caused by poison, and applied on the forehead brings healing. "Hajar al-Had" — it is white with large and coarse granules; it repels poison and strengthens the body; it is beneficial for pregnant women and removes anxiety; it promotes wellbeing and eases ailments. "Hajar al-Khattaf" (swallow stone) — it is found in the nests of swallows and is red; it cures epilepsy, and its red variety cures night terrors. "Hajar al-Millat" — it is also called "Damamij"; it is ground with gray chicken and rooster, sprinkled and used; its wearing cures epilepsy and prevents nightmares.

It was feared that it would stand firm, and its strength along with its brightness would repel animals and pests.
The fat of the human body — in the manner of Adam — arises from illness, and through effort
with the head, it is known that white collyrium removes cataracts from the eye, and when applied it carries away [the ailment] according to tradition.
Oyster shell: it softens worms and removes them; its benefit is for the eyes.
It is said that it means lapis lazuli; every pearl is a jewel, and it benefits joint pains and gout.
And it benefits the eyebrows and eyes, and causes eyelashes to grow well and abundantly. And if
a child in the cradle is given it, and it is struck and sounded, the ear and ox [creature] will come forth.
A sea remedy for the purpose of protecting oneself from being struck by things — thus the sufficient [text] mentions
that it is sufficient when read in the books, in the art of wondrous letters, passed down.
Armion: it is a white stone, streaked with blue, and is fine in appearance.
And as it is broken, its pieces also appear fine. Its fattening quality: in the mine, the result
was that for every weight taken from it, an equal weight of white refined material and its like follow, and beyond this
it is necessarily used when swellings occur; it relieves pain, reduces swellings, and is a carrier of seven properties.
In the eyes of people it appears impressive; it is said to benefit the clouding of the eye. Ithmid al-dhahabi (golden kohl) and its seven kinds
are praised; the golden kind is found in the mine of moderation, and when applied repeatedly, it coats the lids from ignorance.
The other kind, when it has been lacking in the horizon, if redness occurs, it becomes a good remedy and sedative; it does its work thus.
Ithmid al-abyad (white ithmid): it is desired; if it is dry, it protects against poisons and harmful things.
Its temperament is moderately cool and moist, and it benefits clearing of the eyes and removes films.
It profits the eyelids and brightens them, and corrects; and white ithmid likewise benefits and is medicinal, extracted from silver.
It is obtained, and according to physicians, the eyelids and preparations benefit from it greatly.
A white stone like a remedy, and in terms of wonders of creation it is like...

When one looks at the stone of Abadan, so much benefit comes from it that it serves as a remedy for the elite. Muslim scholars have made use of it, composed from the stone, so that the wind may reach them fully. It is able to arrive, and it is a black bird the size of a sparrow; when it passes over settlements it brings benefit; the affliction departs from the stone — Glory be to Him who created all things in wisdom! Some say this stone is found nowhere but in the city of Khasa, and its wall is at the gate, and the town does not bring it to the surrounding areas, so that the stone remains hidden from people's sight, and there is no expenditure from afar of the stone. Its benefit is immense — and God knows best. Borax (būra) is of several types: 1. Armenian borax; 2. Goldsmith's borax; 3. Borax of the gardens; 4. Borax of gold (called bahri); 5. Kermani borax; 6. Western borax. Its colors vary, its temperament is hot and dry in the second degree. Its properties: it treats mange, vitiligo, abscesses, and fissures of the eye; it is indispensable, and if used externally it softens the hand. From the Wonders of Creation: if it is ground, its essence is obtained, and it takes the form of a tablet. It is also found along coasts, and its names are varied — some say it is derived from mine-water; it rises to the surface and forms a crust from which it is collected. It is cold and dry; its smell does not harm the human body, and it is beneficial for a moist constitution. A soft stone obtained by those who walk barefoot: it is found among blacks and dark-complexioned people. It is useful and gives a pleasant fragrance. Turmeric (jaman-jah): its soil is fine; heated by the power of the sun it is used in pressing; its temperament is cold and dry in the third degree. When anointed on the surface it does not allow red pustules to form if red matter is present.

If the assembly (makhluq/setting) is white, the matter will be resolved quickly; if it is black, it will bring salvation; if it is yellow, one will find sweet company among people; if it is notable, the person will be wise; if it is green,
it will be beneficial. Regarding the Hajar Armani (Armenian Stone, i.e., lapis lazuli): lapis lazuli brings vision and virtues; it is helpful for the mind.
Lapis lazuli in various colors is to be used — it brings about change and profit. Regarding the Hajar Asfar (Yellow Stone): if the assembly is white, one will attain one's desire; if it is green, one's work will come about quickly and it will bring answers to questions from people; if it is black, it will become known by the name of whoever carries it without effort. The white stone — it did not remain raw in principle. The Hajar Iblis: there is no place like it; it is a deadly poison but prevents harm in the ascendant of destruction. Regarding hunting with the Hajar Hajin: it is excellent, has a taste like paper, and is among the easy stones. It is useful for pain and in the ascendant it induces sleep. Regarding the Hajar Surkh Sana'i (Red Stone of craft): when placed near someone at night in the surroundings, it makes one sleep. If it is placed under the arm, it will not be lifted. Regarding the Hajar Akhdar (Green Stone): if the assembly is white, it will be found in a place within three days. If it is dug up, its saplings will multiply; if it is black, it will benefit one's household; if it is yellow, it will suit the desires of the people; if it is red, it will be well-spoken of among people; if it is remarkable, whoever is ill will find healing. Regarding the Hajar Abyad (White Stone): if the assembly is complete, its yield will be distinguished from the false; if it is red, all affairs will be resolved; if it is notable, it will erase the character of earthly persons; if the sky/heaven is favorable, the heart will be joyful; if it is green, the benefit will come quickly and it will produce pleasant results; if it contains poison, it will be beneficial. If the assembly is white, something will be found. Regarding the Hajar Insan (Human Stone): if it is black, it will scratch the assembly's fingernails; if it is yellow, it will make the face spotted.

Sanimir is beneficial and repels the harm of bee stings, and twice it is a deterrent against filth.
The terrestrial Mumiyai has fine, light components with warmth, softness, and oiliness as its predominant qualities; its nature is found on the earth like something from Karawat.
It rises through evaporation and emerges from the ground, and its oiliness spreads into the air.
It takes time to appear in the ground at night, and this property is greater then.
Some have called it Water-wax of the Bees and said that its nature according to knowledge is warm and dry.
Its first degree of usefulness: it relieves paralysis, palsy, loss of strength,
epilepsy, headache, and is beneficial for roughness of the tongue, throat constriction, and numbness of the limbs,
and for trembling and palpitations. It is applied topically as described by Mansur, and upon
coming out of it: white and black foam. Its nature is warm and dry.
In the first degree of the fourth part, it is essentially a fine substance, useful for joint pains
and eye ailments and descending water (cataracts). It is beneficial. Worms from the intestinal passage
are expelled by it. The worm passes out. The second rank: Daryanta —
it is produced from the sea creatures, strengthens the senses and movement
and protects the bodily organs, and its components being mixed together
with the male keeps it whole, and if one knowledgeable in compounding knows it, it enters the vessels
and legs and limbs and channels and makes the trees strong; if every
year its channels and legs and vessels remain well-nourished,
and if its composition is not weak, it can sustain itself on its own nourishment.
It grows, and most of it every year from its light produces and multiplies, and Sa'd in its ascendant confirms this.
As has been stated in the discourse of the traveler: "And We spread out the earth — how well We spread it!"

And We brought forth from it grains clustered together, and We brought forth from it palm groves and vineyards, and We caused springs to gush forth from it, so that they might eat of its fruits — and it was not their hands that made all this — will they not then give thanks?

The detailed account of the varieties of plants and their benefits is too extensive to be contained in a single volume. It is well known and has been treated in the books of Shifa, Minhaj, Zanjabil, Kanas al-Lahiyin, Wonders of Creation (Ajaib al-Makhluqat), Taqwim al-Sihhah, Anwar al-Akhbar, Worshidi, and other books of medicine and agriculture. I shall recall and note the forms of things. In the mention of the first form:

The cold tree — its figure is that of a free, upright person, and both the learned and the ignorant have likened it so. The reason for its fruit is that if its nutritive moisture is great but its delicate humors are few, then some of that coarseness remains in the root of the tree, some in the trunk, some makes it dark, and if the delicate humors are few the tree retains its heat — and if there are none it cannot stand upright. But if there are such, the tree becomes firm, giving nourishment and starch to those around it.

As for the qualities of its wood: it is straight and good in nature, and in its fiber there resides a power — yet its nutritive essence draws water upward from below by reason of its height. The tree holds its branches upright and keeps them in place. This delicate quality causes it to bind the parts together so that each part becomes part of the tree itself, and it drives out the excess through the bark; but the nutritive power that remains is what brings about the manifestation of the roots of the tree, its leaves and its flowers. By this the attracting power draws nourishment and the formative power gives it shape, and the retaining power holds it, and the growing power increases and extends it. In this creation there are wonders — and blessed and exalted is the Maker — and some of the finest of His creation give praise, nourishing even the least of creatures.

Nasadwan called the fortresses "Masinar" by layers, and also Sanud, and the river Hanw and Bada, and Funduq and Shiq and Ban and white Musk and their like, and Hindi is known by its outward appearance. Despite its extreme delicateness, over time, for this reason, all the Alma ibn Mubarak are consumed. How the bone in the middle is found, and its fine marrow within, turned yellow like fenugreek. And the Shaftalwa and Alwa — no one understands it, and each resembles in form the white Hudhud and the Peel. The marrow within resembles apple and Marw and others like them, and some in the quality of the bone give marrow like dates and reeds and Nitun and Unab and apple. And Sajd and their like, and meaning: in the depth of the bone the marrow appears together in form. Like Anjubar and Kafsh and Mulberry and their like — in every form it is like the original. And the quality of its appearance is founded and the statement of the expert testifies: "We say: there is no god but God, for love and repentance brings the living out from the dead, and brings the dead out from the living — this is God." And if they say reconciliation, the pillars are established tall, so that it gives him provision and support and turns it. The roots of the trees are firm in it, and by the power of the sap, the yellow and the limbs gain increase. Its leaves and fruit are black, and the fruit of the other leaves passes over it gently with its leaves. It was thus established, so that the milk of fig comes, and those creatures arrive, and meaning: the detail of the design of Anbaz and the explanation — so that the cooperation is not given. In that is a clear sign for a people who reflect. Now the detail of the types of fruit trees, as is well known, and the form of Samar and Anzad, and whatever is famous by name — we will mention its name and species and well-known attributes, with ease. We will describe the first form: on the mention of the fruit trees of Samar and those like it, of Sha't and Nabunakh in the castles — as mentioned in the books of agriculture, that the tree from its roots gives yield, and its character is thus established.

The tree came into contact and alignment, and the bones joined with bones, completing [the treatment]. This [substance] repels the effects of poisons and preserves life from death. The scholars have acknowledged that its imam [chief property] is to sustain and spread knowledge generally, and it was noted that it was occupied in its nature, saying: "Travel is the time for study, and this is the grace of God." When mixed with almond oil and the planets [are favorable], it benefits the heart. Muhammad — may God have mercy on him — recorded it: it is warm and dry in the first degree, moist in the second, and its temperament is moderate. If it is mixed with oil and applied to the hair, it will protect against poison and be useful. According to Al-Mufid, it is beneficial: it strengthens the teeth and gums. The Arabs call it a worm [type], and it is dry, beneficial to the body, and its green color is white as coral, black in consistency; it builds up the organs. It has a pleasant scent; when placed in the ear, it induces good hearing and stops bleeding. If swallowed, it relieves bladder pain and cools the body, and has a pleasant fragrance. If crushed and mixed with honey and buried at the root of a tree, it accelerates the tree's natural growth. Cold and dry in the second degree: its water freshens the breath, benefits the sight, relieves paralysis, and if placed among diamonds, it protects against the harm of paralysis. Its extract repels animal poisons, and if its concentrate is applied to the eyes, it sharpens vision, repels cataracts, and eliminates cloudiness.

Marginalia:
Barqaf
Bosansh [note]

It relieves sciatica and is beneficial for the digestive system; it is from the fifth [category], originating from the Indian region. It calms epileptic episodes in women, and if given to a nursing woman, it benefits her.

[Regarding] amchas: Take a moderate amount of Isfahan mint, use it in a dry and cold manner; it is beneficial for the second degree. If used [in excess], it causes the stomach to emit gas, and when cooked, it dries the phlegm in the chest and intestines.

It expels corrupt matter, clears the bile from the liver, and removes corrupt substances; this is stated in the writings of scholars.

When made fresh and ground, [the plant called] Azad Darakhsh is useful as described by the authors; it is known that it is a good antidote to poisons, and it does not cause harm. Wherever it is consumed, it acts as a diuretic, removes hair, and is beneficial for the spleen.

With honey it repels worms from the body, and it is given in the measure of two dirhams. It is cold and moist in the second degree, reduces fever, and has a moderating effect.

But sanbiya [a plant] is of two kinds: one softens and aids digestion, and does not cause harm.

[Regarding] amich: It is first taken with warm water; it is useful against constipation, gout, and senna. It can be taken frequently; it purifies bile and cleanses the body. Mixed with other [substances] it is laxative, and mixed with haldila [myrobalan] it more easily induces gentle laxation.

As for its nature, it is necessarily among beneficial substances whose existence is mandatory; it is among the recognized medicines. It acts as an astringent when taken with haldila, and it destroys worms and dryness.

It is used both externally and internally; internally it is protective. In the brain it causes sneezing, benefits the head, and helps against many dangers.

It eliminates intestinal worms and its extract serves as a repellent; it is of the highest benefit. From the water of Ban there are two varieties: Manū and Anā. The tree of Manū resembles silver in appearance, its bark is like that of silk, and it is fragrant; it is from the highlands of Khurasan among the people there. It treats skin conditions such as herpes, and when dried it benefits vitiligo, blemishes, freckles, skin eruptions, and toothaches; mixed with lemon it is beneficial. Bṭīmīr and dried cinnamon — the fresh form of it was more common before, and it warms and dries; it benefits paralysis, facial palsy, excessive food accumulation in the stomach, and is useful for purging; its resin is of the highest grade; some say it tightens the gums, is beneficial in warfare, thickens bodily humors, and promotes hair growth. Baqam is well known; its fruit is sharp and cuts leeches. In the lands of India and Sind it is very common; it is used in festivals and perfumes, and is employed in various ways. In hot regions it is dry; it benefits paralysis and facial palsy and is useful against cold reptiles and animals; it reduces phlegm; it is known in their lands as māṭarḥ, and from it a fine water is produced. It is used mixed with refined white material; it is warm and dry; it benefits facial palsy, vertigo, and digestion; it dissolves corrupt wounds, removes paralysis, repels insects and animals, relieves dysuria, urinary retention, and is useful for treatment. The blossom of this tree produces an oil, and the oil obtained from it is powerful; it kills worms at sunrise; it purges the bowels, and when this oil is rubbed onto the udders of animals, it causes them to increase their yield, though only by a small amount.

The balsam tree grows in that land, along with roses, sugar, musk, myrrh, and ambergris. It benefits those who use it when rain falls on it, as it draws out the venom of scorpions and provides protection. Every tree that lacks water has no such virtue in place of sugar. The pomegranate with its rind is cold and dry, its skin is used as an astringent, and its juice is beneficial. Its kernels are sweet as honey; the sour pomegranate strengthens the gums. Its peel is useful and aids digestion; its seeds benefit the liver and help with urinary flow. Placing its branches prevents blight, and its virtues drive away bile and intestinal worms, purify the blood, and reduce fatigue.

Abbas reported: I heard the Prophet say, "Eat the pomegranate with its white pith, for it tans the stomach and there is not a single seed that enters a man's belly but that it illuminates his heart and silences Satan's whispering for forty days." When drunk by a noble person it is beneficial; taken with milk it is even better. Mastic mixed with pomegranate is also good.

As for the date palm — it is blessed and greatly beneficial. It aids digestion of food and drink. God Most High mentioned it in the Quran and Hudhayfah reported that the Prophet said: "Honor your aunt the date palm, for it was created from the same clay as Adam." And the tongue in its heart — ask God the Exalted — Gabriel descended with it, and it is at the rank of the blessed tree.

A command was given: take from them all, keeping them in mind, drawing safety from every harm. Regarding peace and greed: apply the ruling — it is narrated that "vinegar is an excellent condiment." And from the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Use olive oil, for it cures pain, removes phlegm, strengthens the nerves, lifts burdens, improves character, gladdens the soul, and dispels heaviness." The oil of the olive tree, if applied to a wound on a tree — the olive tree in particular — and rubbed, will benefit. If a little is applied regularly, it removes pain and is beneficial. Its properties have been recorded: it is used as a remedy and clears head pain. Storax, if taken, removes intestinal worms and is beneficial. When rubbed warmly it is a good remedy. When mixed with fine substances it nourishes and strengthens. When used with Indian pepper it is sought by those who desire it. A little of it mixed together gives strength and is beneficial to the digestion. Adding sugar to it — its oil softens the skin and protects from cold. It relieves inflammation, dryness, and pain, and strengthens the faculties of the brain. Its flesh moistens the teeth and is sought by those who need it. It is cold and moist in the first degree, dry and cold, and is beneficial. If bound with chickpeas soaked in water it is better, and if its seeds are soaked in milk and applied to the roots of a tree and rubbed in the right place on the head, it strengthens hard hair and prevents its falling out.

It removes the bitterness; it is moderately warm and dry, and counters bile-induced diarrhea and weakness. It strengthens the constitution and keeps the temperament restrained and soft. Safarhal is called by name among the cold simples, cold in the first degree. Yahya ibn Talha related on the authority of Dhayba that the Messenger of God gave it and said: "O Muhammad, it heals the heart of sickness and sorrow." And from the Messenger it was reported likewise. It was also reported on the authority of Ja'far al-Tayyar that he gave it and said: "Eat it, for its color and taste are fine." It quells appetite for harmful things, settles fevers, and gives strength to the faculties, and relieves itching. It settles flatulence, and if a pregnant woman eats it, her child will be well-tempered, pleasant-natured, and sweet-smelling. And if a nursing woman drinks it mixed with honey it benefits further, and given to a household it prevents excessive loose bowels, and the seed of the fustuq al-rayr settles coughs. Sabestan is well-known; it benefits the throat, the gullet, and the stomach, and expels black-bile humors. Its ruling: it is astringent, and it is well known that it is cold; it is like stone in its coldness. The mountain tree does not lose its leaves in autumn at all. It strengthens the stomach, gives it vigor, and benefits the intestines from saffron. It strengthens the senses, prevents harm, and is generally beneficial. Sandrus: its tree is well known; its gum is like that of the pine, soft; its heat expels worms in the second degree; and from it a resin is extracted. Oil of Sandrus, known as a constrictive agent, checks epilepsy, hemorrhoids, and [illegible].

It is truly among the most beneficial things — the chestnut (Shah Balut) is well known. In terms of heat and dryness it is less than the oak. Its taste is less intense; it is given to strengthen the constitution and produces dryness. It repels poisons, stops bleeding, and is beneficial for the intestines. The pine (Sanawbar) is well known. Its taste is warm, given to strengthen the constitution. Some say it comes from the larch tree of Khurasan, and others say that it grows in a certain region of the lowlands and hilly terrain. In the wood of the pine there is a resinous substance — when fresh, if a torch is made from it, it burns with great flame and smoke, and its resin resembles mastic; in Arabic it is called the almond of the throat (tonsil). If it is pounded and its decoction drunk with animals and kept, and from its extract a fine paste is made — if gargled with vinegar it removes tooth pain and toothache, strengthens sexual potency, its fumes benefit the nerves, repel serpents, and are useful against scorpion venom. Especially mixed with ginger, walnut, and dates, it corrects the constitution of the muscles. The mountain variety is said to be close to it in nature. It is warm and of moderate dryness; it repels poisons, removes harmful winds from the body, aids digestion, and benefits the bowels. These meanings have been composed in verse. The juniper, used pure ♦ — it is said that it is known to bring forth a stillborn child ♦ — when cut it splits open ♦ — its grit is used in construction. The meaning said is that it is like sugar; others have called it a type of grain and reckoned it among the grains. It corrects straight from the trunk; it is warm, given to strengthen, and expels phlegm and dryness. The Arab scholars have recorded it: it repels weakness, strengthens the organs, and is beneficial in the wonders of creation — mention of which has been made since the time of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic era).

The Arabs, whenever one wished to ascertain something in the household, would twist two of its branches together, and when they returned, if the branches remained twisted in the same manner, it was a sign of the chastity of the household of the Shimr family; otherwise it would be the opposite. Jujube (unab) is well known. First degree: it is beneficial for the chest and for nourishing children when used in that way. It is useful for ailments of the eye, stops nosebleeds, and gives freshness. It moistens the back when pressed as a poultice. It prevents the blood. Among the properties of jujube: it stirs the blood when made into a hot infusion and brings it out. It is harmful to the stomach. Oud (agarwood) is well known. Its smoke and fumes repel great poisons and strengthening aromatic pastes. It is dry in the second degree. In the regions where it is used, it serves as a moist agent; it is known that it is made as a good quality product. It surpasses manufactured varieties in this way, as is shown by the fragrance that rises from it. It benefits the heart, strengthens it, and benefits the organs and removes harmful wastes, eliminates winds, calms pain, and soothes the interior. It is called a digestive and is known to be good for the teeth and is pleasantly fragrant. It is of the second degree, better in its aroma and fragrance than pepper. It freshens the breath, strengthens the stomach, and aids digestion. Ambergris (anbar) is of the first degree. Though it comes from Baldūm and however many varieties exist, the closer it is to shore, the better. Aloe (sabar) is raw in its nature. It is placed in houses to be used, and from its flowering, people benefit. It expels what causes grief, and acts as a laxative. It strengthens alertness, and its yellow color is beneficial for children. Mastic (mastiq) is well known and warm.

In sum, it is first dry and cold in temperament, and in Turkish it is called "juwbish"; it is a reliable remedy. Its common use firms up the gums, repels poison from the body, and strengthens sexual desire and potency. It is beneficial for pleurisy, eliminates mucus, and removes blemishes. It purges phlegm from the body, and its oil, when applied as kohl to the eyes, clears cloudiness of vision and removes two close friends [i.e., two ailments]. It drives away fever. Pepper: its temperament is warm and dry, of the first degree. From its worms one should use the bark found among them; the means of pepper is pepper itself, which is warming, and it eliminates cold diseases in the body, and cures night blindness when used as kohl, and is beneficial for the eyes. Applying it as a liniment warms the body, strengthens sexual potency, and pepper relieves palpitations and hardness. It promotes urination and clears cloudiness of vision, aids digestion, and prevents women from conceiving after intercourse. The branches of pepper are known by this name; it is beneficial against cold winds.

Cubeb: it is cold and dry in the second degree, and it soothes grief and pain; it is useful. Red coral: it is warm and dry in the first degree; it eliminates scratching. Its benefit is that it strengthens the liver, and when it is prepared and made powerful, it is beneficial for the spleen. It is effective against freckles, spots on the face, hemorrhoids, and improves vision. Hazelnut: it is well known, warm in temperament, of the first degree. In the Book of Wonders it is recorded that if hazelnut shells are placed in a room, those inside cannot breathe. It nourishes the brain, and its oil, when applied as kohl to a child with blue eyes, blackens the eyes. Pregnant women should grind scorpion [some ingredient] and rub it on [the skin]; it makes the hair grow.
